vignette:
Patient: Maria, 39-year-old married female, Latin American, active-duty soldier  
Trauma Type: Natural disaster (earthquake)  
PCL-5: 65  

Maria sits at the edge of the chair, back straight, hands resting on her knees as if she’s waiting for an order. She’s a staff sergeant in the Army, and every part of her posture says ready. But her eyes tell a different story—they flicker to the window, then to the door, then back to me. She apologizes twice for being late, even though she was early.

She tells me about the earthquake. It was two years ago, during a deployment in a mountainous region. She was leading a convoy through a narrow valley when the ground began to roll. At first, she thought it was an IED. That’s what soldiers think. But then the road split open in front of her vehicle, and the mountain on her left began to fall.

“I remember the sound,” she says. “Not the shaking. The sound. Like the whole world was chewing itself apart.”

She ordered her team to dismount, to take cover. She pulled a private from the back of a Humvee seconds before a boulder crushed it. She remembers the private’s name—Martinez. He was nineteen. He cried. She told him to shut up and move. She didn’t mean to be harsh, she says, but there was no time.

For six hours, they were trapped. The road was gone. The radio was dead. She had to keep her squad calm, keep them from panicking, keep them from drinking their water too fast. She checked on each of them, counted them again and again. She remembers the taste of dust. She remembers the smell of diesel and blood—though no one in her squad was bleeding. It was an animal, she thinks. A deer, maybe.

Now, back home, Maria cannot stop counting. She counts the tiles in my office ceiling. She counts the steps from her car to the front door. She counts her husband’s breaths at night because if she doesn’t, she’s sure he’ll stop.

She has not slept through the night since the earthquake. She wakes at 3:17 a.m.—the exact time the shaking stopped—and lies still, listening. She checks the windows. She checks the doors. She runs her hand along the walls to make sure they’re solid. Her husband, a civilian, has learned not to touch her when she wakes. “He reached for me once,” she says. “I almost broke his wrist.”

At work, she is still a good soldier. Her evaluations are excellent. But she volunteers for every night shift, every extra detail. She cannot sit still. When she is idle, she hears the mountain. When she closes her eyes, she sees Martinez’s face. She has not told anyone that she sometimes cannot remember the way home from the base, that she has driven past her exit three times in one week, that she has to write down the simplest tasks because her mind goes blank.

She avoids the news. She avoids rain. She avoids the sound of heavy trucks. Last month, a forklift dropped a pallet in the motor pool, and she dove behind a crate. Her soldiers laughed. She laughed too. But her hands were shaking for an hour.

Maria says she came to see me because her husband told her she was “different.” She says it’s nothing. She says she’s fine. But she has already checked the window three times, and she hasn’t finished telling me her name.
